docs.title: FortiGate Firewall – Block Social Media Websites (GUI)
FortiGate Firewall – Block Social Media Websites Using (GUI)
Overview
docs.text: FortiGate Web Filter allows network administrators to block access to specific websites like: www.youtube.com, www.facebook.com, www.instagram.com, domains, and URL paths.

docs.title: Configuration workflow
docs.text: Step 1         Create URL Filter Profile         Step 2         Apply Web Filter Profile         to Firewall Policy         Step 3         Test & Verify

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Web Filter Profile
docs.text:
1. Log in to the FortiGate GUI.

  2. Navigate to Security Profiles → Web Filter.

  3. Click Create New.

  4. Enter the profile name: Block-Social-Media.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Static URL Filter
docs.text:
Inside the new Web Filter profile:

  1. Find the Static URL Filter section.

  2. Enable URL Filter.

  3. Click Create New for each website.

  4. Add the following entries:

URL Type Action Status *youtube.com Wildcard Block Enable *facebook.com Wildcard Block Enable *instagram.com Wildcard Block Enable Purpose: Adds the social media websites to the URL block list.

Use the following example configuration: (Screenshot):

docs.title: Step 3: Apply the Profile to the Firewall Policy
docs.text:
A URL filter will not protect users unless the applicable traffic passes through a firewall policy with the Web Filter profile enabled.

  1. Go to Policy & Objects → Firewall Policy.

  2. Identify the policy that allows users to access the internet.

  3. Edit that policy.

  4. Enable Security Profiles or UTM Inspection, depending on the FortiOS version.

  5. Enable Web Filter.

  6. Select the profile Block-Social-Media.

  7. Enable SSL/SSH inspection as appropriate for your network.

  8. Save the policy.

Important: Edit the correct internet access policy. Do not change unrelated policies.

Use the following example configuration: (Screenshot):

docs.title: Step 4: Test the Configuration
docs.text:
1. Connect a client computer to the network.

  2. Open YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.

  3. Confirm that the websites are blocked.

  4. If YouTube videos still play, check HTTPS inspection, QUIC/HTTP/3 traffic, and whether the correct firewall policy is being used.

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram should be blocked for users whose internet traffic passes through the configured firewall policy. Websites not matched by a blocking rule should remain accessible.

Note: GUI menu names can differ between FortiOS versions. Configuration must be tested on a client device to confirm that blocking is working.

docs.title: Check Web Filter logs
docs.text:
If the website is still accessible, check the logs:

  1. Navigate to Log & Report → Security Events.

  2. Open the Web Filter events.

  3. Filter for the client's source IP address or the destination hostname.

  4. Review the action, matched URL, profile, and policy ID.

  5. Look for an entry with an action such as blocked and a message indicating that the URL matched the local URL filter.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: FortiGate firewalls also allow administrators to block Web Filter feature and firewall policies using graphical user interface (GUI) as well as Command Line Interface (CLI).

docs.title: Step 1: Create the URL Filter Table
docs.text:
1. Log in to the FortiGate firewall using SSH, a console connection, or the CLI Console available in the web interface.

  2. First, create a URL filter table and add a rule to block social media sites.

config webfilter urlfilter
    edit 1
        set name "Social-Media-URLs"
        config entries
            edit 1
                set url "*youtube.com"
                set type wildcard
                set action block
            next
            edit 2
                set url "*facebook.com"
                set type wildcard
                set action block
            next
            edit 3
                set url "*instagram.com"
                set type wildcard
                set action block
            next
        end
    next
end

Purpose: Creates a URL Filter table containing the websites to be blocked.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure the Web Filter Profile
docs.text:
config webfilter profile
    edit "Block-Social-Media"
        config web
            set urlfilter-table 1
        end
    next
end

Purpose: Links URL Filter table ID 1 to the Block-Social-Media profile.

docs.title: Step 3: Apply the Profile to the Firewall Policy
docs.text:
First, identify the firewall policy used for internet access:

show firewall policy

Use the actual policy ID in the following commands. The example below uses policy ID 1.

config firewall policy
    edit 1
        set utm-status enable
        set webfilter-profile "Block-Social-Media"
    next
end

Purpose: Enables security inspection and applies the custom Web Filter profile to the selected firewall policy.

Important: Modify the correct internet access policy to avoid affecting other network traffic.

docs.title: Step 4: Verify the Configuration
docs.text:
Check the URL Filter table

show webfilter urlfilter

Check the Web Filter profile

show webfilter profile "Block-Social-Media"

Check the firewall policy

show firewall policy

Confirm that the correct policy has the following settings

set utm-status enable
set webfilter-profile "Block-Social-Media"

docs.title: Expected Result
docs.text:
• YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram should be blocked for users whose traffic passes through the configured firewall policy.

  • The custom Web Filter profile should be applied to the correct policy.

  • Test the websites from a client computer to confirm that blocking works.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If YouTube videos still play after applying the configuration, check HTTPS inspection, QUIC/HTTP/3 traffic, and whether the traffic is actually passing through the configured policy.

Note: Configuration alone does not guarantee successful blocking. Always test and verify the result on the client device.

docs.title: Important Consideration:
docs.text:
1. Correct Policy ID: Verify that you are modifying the correct LAN-to-WAN firewall policy handling the client's traffic.

  2. Profile Association: Ensure the Static URL Filter list is linked to the intended Web Filter profile and that the profile is applied to the relevant firewall policies.

  3. Wildcard Matching: Configure URL patterns carefully, such as *facebook.com, because matching behavior may vary with the pattern and FortiOS version.

  4. HTTPS Inspection: URL filtering capabilities depend on the SSL inspection profile and the visibility available for encrypted traffic.

  5. Additional Domains: Applications may use additional domains, content delivery networks (CDNs), and alternate endpoints. Blocking one domain may not block the entire application.

  6. QUIC and HTTP/3: These protocols can affect filtering behavior. Review QUIC handling if blocking is incomplete.

  7. Existing Configuration: Review existing firewall and security profiles before making changes to avoid overwriting required settings.

  8. FortiOS Compatibility: Confirm command syntax and supported features for your FortiGate FortiOS version.

  9. Production Deployment: Test changes in a controlled environment before applying them to production networks.

Official Reference: Fortinet's FortiOS 7.4.8 Administration Guide. Your interface may differ slightly. Reference Source: Fortinet — Static URL Filter and verification

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Blocking a website on FortiGate using CLI involves three main tasks: configuring a Static URL Filter, associating it with a Web Filter profile, and applying that profile to the appropriate firewall policy.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: To establish a formal procedure for the daily management, maintenance, and operational integrity of the Property Management System (PMS), ensuring seamless Front Office operations, system availability, and accurate guest data management.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This SOP applies to all members of the IT Department responsible for administering, monitoring, securing, maintaining, and troubleshooting the Property Management System (PMS) and its integrated systems.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
• Execution: IT Manager and IT Executive.

  • Monitoring: IT Manager.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Perform a daily system health check of the PMS server, connected terminals, and associated services.

  2. Verify the successful completion of the nightly audit and scheduled data backups.

  3. Review system logs for errors, warnings, unusual activities, and unauthorized access attempts.

  4. Monitor PMS integrations, including the Point of Sale (POS), key card system, and Private Branch Exchange (PBX), to confirm that all interfaces are online and communicating correctly.

  5. Create, modify, and deactivate PMS user accounts according to approved requests and employee roles.

  6. Verify that appropriate access permissions are assigned to authorized personnel based on their job responsibilities.

  7. Coordinate with the Front Office and Reservations teams to investigate and resolve PMS-related issues promptly.

  8. Record all PMS incidents, troubleshooting activities, and corrective actions in the IT ticketing system.

  9. Apply approved software patches and updates during off-peak hours, following vendor recommendations and change management procedures.

  10. Verify system functionality after maintenance or updates and confirm that critical PMS services are operating normally.

  11. Escalate major incidents, recurring errors, and potential data integrity issues to the IT Manager and relevant stakeholders.

  12. Maintain daily health check reports, access records, maintenance logs, and backup verification records.

docs.title: Standards & Guidelines
docs.text:
• PMS access must be granted according to the principle of least privilege and business requirements.

  • Routine maintenance should be scheduled during low-occupancy or off-peak periods to minimize operational disruption.

  • The target PMS system availability should be 99.9% or higher, subject to approved service requirements and vendor capabilities.

  • All PMS-related incidents, service requests, and changes must be documented in the IT ticketing system.

  • Software updates and configuration changes must be authorized and performed according to approved change management procedures.

  • User accounts must be reviewed periodically, and access must be revoked promptly when no longer required.

  • Data backups must be monitored regularly, and restoration procedures should be tested according to the hotel's backup policy.

  • Any suspected security incident or guest data exposure must be reported immediately through the hotel's incident escalation process.

docs.title: Records & Documentation
docs.text:
The following records must be maintained:

  • Daily PMS system health check reports.

  • IT ticketing system logs for PMS-related incidents and service requests.

  • PMS user access records and change logs.

  • Nightly audit verification reports.

  • Data backup completion and verification reports.

  • Software update and maintenance records.

  • PMS incident investigation and resolution reports.

  • System availability and downtime records.

docs.title: Safety & Precautions
docs.text:
• Never share, disclose, or reuse PMS login credentials in an unauthorized manner.

  • Use strong passwords and approved authentication controls wherever supported.

  • Handle guest information with strict confidentiality and in accordance with applicable data protection requirements and hotel policies.

  • Do not make unauthorized changes to PMS configurations, user permissions, or integrated systems.

  • Verify backup completion before performing maintenance that could affect system data or availability.

  • Maintenance requiring system downtime must be communicated in advance and approved by the General Manager and relevant Department Heads.

  • Follow the hotel's incident response and escalation procedures in the event of system failure, suspected unauthorized access, or data loss.

  • Ensure that critical PMS functions are verified after maintenance before returning the system to normal operation.

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text: To protect the resort’s network and computing infrastructure from malware, viruses, and unauthorized data transfers through effective antivirus protection and USB device management.

docs.title: 2. Scope
docs.text: This SOP applies to all IT Department personnel and covers all resort-owned computing devices, including servers, desktops, laptops, and Point of Sale (POS) terminals.

docs.title: 3. Responsibility
docs.text:
• Execution: IT Executive

  • Monitoring and Compliance: IT Manager

docs.title: 4.1 Antivirus Management
docs.text:
1. Ensure that approved antivirus software is installed and active on all resort-owned computing devices.

  2. Update antivirus definitions automatically wherever possible, or perform manual updates when required.

  3. Perform weekly full system scans on all mission-critical servers and desktops.

  4. Monitor the centralized antivirus management console for security alerts, detected threats, quarantined files, and scan status.

  5. Investigate and remediate detected threats according to the resort’s IT security procedures.

  6. Immediately isolate any device suspected of being infected to prevent the spread of malware across the network.

docs.title: 4.2 USB Device Management
docs.text:
1. Disable USB autorun functionality on all applicable resort-owned computing devices.

  2. Permit only IT-approved, scanned, and whitelisted USB storage devices.

  3. Scan every USB storage device using approved antivirus software before accessing or transferring files.

  4. Prohibit the use of personal or unauthorized USB storage devices on resort computers.

  5. Maintain an official whitelist of approved USB devices, including device identification details and authorization status.

  6. Remove or revoke authorization for USB devices that are lost, compromised, or no longer required.

docs.title: 5. Standards & Guidelines
docs.text:
• Antivirus definitions must be updated at least once every 24 hours.

  • Antivirus protection must remain enabled and operational on all supported devices.

  • Weekly full system scans must be completed and documented for mission-critical servers and desktops.

  • Devices with detected or suspected malware must be isolated from the network immediately, following established incident response procedures.

  • Personal and unauthorized USB storage devices must not be connected to resort-owned computers.

  • Only authorized and whitelisted USB devices may be used for business purposes.

  • The IT Department must maintain an up-to-date USB device whitelist.

  • Any antivirus failure, suspicious activity, or security incident must be reported promptly to the IT Manager.

docs.title: 6. Records & Documentation
docs.text:
The IT Department must maintain the following records:

  • Centralized antivirus console reports, including detected threats, quarantined files, and scan history.

  • Antivirus definition update logs and records of manual updates.

  • Full system scan logs and remediation records.

  • Approved USB device whitelist and authorization records.

  • Security incident reports and corrective actions taken.

docs.title: 7. Safety & Precautions
docs.text:
1. In the event of a suspected malware outbreak, immediately isolate affected devices from the network to prevent lateral spread.

  2. Do not delete quarantined files or disable antivirus protection without proper authorization.

  3. Do not connect unknown, personal, or unapproved USB storage devices to resort-owned computers.

  4. Report serious security incidents immediately to the IT Manager and General Manager.

  5. Preserve relevant security logs and evidence for investigation, where applicable.

docs.title: 8. Compliance
docs.text: All IT personnel must follow this SOP. Any exception to antivirus or USB security controls requires prior authorization from the IT Manager and must be documented.

docs.title: What is Computer Network?
docs.text:
A computer network is a group of components or other devices connected together to communicate, exchange data, and share resources such as files, printers, applications, and an internet connection.

Example: Computers connected to the same Wi-Fi network in an office can share files and access a common printer.

docs.title: Importance of network
docs.text:
• Easy sharing of files & information
  • Sharing of expensive device like Servers, Printers

docs.title: Network components
docs.text:
• End Devices: Computers, servers, printers, and smartphones.
  • Network devices: Hub, Modem, Switch, Router, Repeater, Network Interface Card (NIC), Bridge, Wi-Fi Access Point, Firewall.
  • Transmission media: Ethernet cables, fiber-optic cables, and Wireless.
  • Protocols: TCP/IP, HTTP, FTP, DNS, SMTP and Telnet.

docs.title: Network Topology
docs.text:
Network topology is the physical or logical arrangement of computers, network devices, and communication links within a computer network.

In simple words, network topology describes how network devices are connected to each other and how data travels between them.

docs.title: 1. Star Topology
docs.text:
All devices connect to a central switch or hub.

  1. Easy to manage and troubleshoot.
  2. A central device failure can affect the entire network.

Example: Office LAN.

docs.title: 2. Bus Topology
docs.text:
All devices share one main backbone cable.

  • Uses less cable.
  • A backbone failure can disrupt the network.

![[Pasted image 20261019175911.png|247]]

Example: Older Ethernet networks.

docs.title: 3. Ring Topology
docs.text:
1. Each device connects to two neighboring devices, forming a loop.

  2. Data can travel around the ring.

  3. A single link failure may disrupt a basic, unprotected ring.

![[Pasted image 20261019180041.png|219]]

Example: Some legacy ring networks.

docs.title: 4. Mesh Topology
docs.text:
Devices have multiple interconnections. In a full mesh, every device connects directly to every other device.

  1. High redundancy and reliability.
  2. Expensive and complex to implement.

![[Pasted image 20261019180935.png|226]]

Example: Redundant WAN connections.

docs.title: 5. Tree Topology
docs.text:
Devices are arranged in a hierarchical structure with branches.

  1. Easy to expand and organize.
  2. Failure of an upper-level device can affect its branches.

![[Pasted image 20261019181126.png|280]]

Example: Enterprise campus network.

docs.title: 6. Hybrid Topology
docs.text:
Combines two or more different topologies.

  1. Flexible and scalable.
  2. Design and troubleshooting can be more complex.

![[Pasted image 20261019181257.png|325]]

Example: A company combining star LANs with a redundant backbone.

docs.title: Physical Topology
docs.text:
Physical topology refers to the actual physical arrangement of network devices, cables, ports, and other hardware components in a network.

In simple words, it describes how devices are physically connected to each other.

docs.title: Logical Topology
docs.text:
Logical topology refers to how data flows between devices across a network, regardless of the physical arrangement of the devices and cables.

In simple words, it describes how devices communicate and how data travels through the network.

docs.title: 1. LAN(Local Area Network)
docs.text: A high-speed network confined to a small geographic area (e.g., office, building) using Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) or Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) for data transmission. Typically managed by a single organization.

docs.title: 2. WAN(Wide area Network)
docs.text: A geographically distributed network that interconnects LANs over large distances using leased lines (e.g., MPLS, Metro Ethernet) or public networks (e.g., Internet with VPN tunneling). Security mechanisms such as IPSec or SSL/TLS are often implemented.

docs.title: 3. MAN(Metropolitan Area Network)
docs.text: A network that spans a city or campus area, often owned by ISPs or large enterprises. Uses technologies like Ethernet MAN, DWDM, or microwave transmission.

docs.title: 4. Personal Area Network (PAN)
docs.text: A short-range network used for personal devices (e.g., smartphones, wearables) using Bluetooth, ZigBee, or USB interconnects.

docs.title: 5. Virtual Private Network (VPN)
docs.text: A secure overlay network built over a public infrastructure (usually the Internet), providing encrypted tunnels (e.g., IPSec, SSL-VPN) for secure remote access.

docs.title: Communication Media
docs.text:
Communication media is the physical path or wireless medium through which data travels from one network device to another.

In simple words, communication media is the medium that carries data between devices in a network.

Example Connection of a computer to a switch using an Ethernet cable, the cable acts as the communication medium.

docs.title: Types of Communication Media
docs.text: Communication media is divided into two main categories.

docs.title: 1. Guided Media (Wired)
docs.text:
Data travels through a physical cable.

Examples: Twisted-pair cable, coaxial cable, fiber-optic cable.

docs.title: 2. Unguided Media (Wireless)
docs.text:
Data travels through electromagnetic waves without a physical cable.

Examples: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular radio, satellite communication.

docs.title: A. Twisted Pair Cable (UTP/STP)
docs.text:
A cable containing pairs of insulated copper wires twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference.

  • UTP: Unshielded Twisted Pair
  • STP: Shielded Twisted Pair
  • Common categories: Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6A
  • Common Ethernet channel length: up to 100 metres, depending on the standard and installation.

![[Pasted image 20261019183731.png|318]]

docs.title: B. Coaxial Cable
docs.text:
A cable with a central conductor, insulation, metallic shielding, and an outer jacket.

  • Good shielding against interference.
  • Used in cable television and some broadband access networks.
  • Less common for modern Ethernet LAN connections.

![[Pasted image 20261019184118.png|405]]

docs.title: C. Fiber-Optic Cable
docs.text:
Transmits data using light pulses through glass or plastic fibers.

  • Single-mode fiber (SMF): Common for long-distance links.
  • Multimode fiber (MMF): Common for shorter links, such as within buildings and data centers.
  • High bandwidth and immunity to electromagnetic interference.

![[Pasted image 20261019184231.png|293]]

docs.title: 2. Unguided Media (Wireless Communication)
docs.text:
Data is transmitted through the air or vacuum using electromagnetic waves.

  • Radio Waves (Wi-Fi, LTE):
    • Omni-directional, subject to interference and eavesdropping.
    • Requires encryption (e.g., WPA3, IPSec) for secure communication.
  • Microwave Transmission:
    • Line-of-sight; used in point-to-point communication.
    • Prone to weather-related attenuation.
  • Infrared:
    • Short-range, line-of-sight.
    • Common in remote controls and some sensor networks.
  • Satellite Communication:
    • Long-distance, global coverage.
    • High latency, vulnerable to interception and weather.

docs.title: OSI Reference Model
docs.text:
The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) Model is a conceptual framework developed by the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) that standardizes the functions of a telecommunication or computing system into seven abstract layers. It facilitates interoperability, troubleshooting, and security implementation across diverse systems and protocols by providing a common language and structure for network communication.

1. Physical Layer: Deals with the physical connection and transmission of raw binary data over a medium. Includes cables, switches, and network interface cards.

  1. Data Link Layer: Manages node-to-node data transfer, error detection, and correction. Includes MAC addresses and switches.

3. Network Layer: Handles logical addressing and routing of data packets between networks. Includes IP addresses and routers.

4. Transport Layer: Ensures reliable data transfer with error checking and flow control. Includes TCP and UDP protocols.

5. Session Layer: Manages sessions or connections between applications. Controls dialogues and data exchange.

6. Presentation Layer: Translates data between the application layer and the network format. Handles encryption, decryption, and data compression.

7.Application Layer: Provides network services directly to end-user applications. Includes protocols like HTTP, FTP, and SMTP.

Layer Name Function Examples Security Focus 7 Application Interface for user applications HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS Input validation, authentication, app-layer firewalls 6 Presentation Data formatting, encryption/decryption, compression SSL/TLS, JPEG, ASCII, EBCDIC Data encryption, encoding 5 Session Establishes, manages, and terminates sessions NetBIOS, RPC Session tokens, timeout policies 4 Transport Reliable delivery, segmentation, flow control TCP, UDP Port filtering, session hijacking protection 3 Network Logical addressing and routing IP, ICMP, OSPF IP filtering, packet inspection, VPN tunneling 2 Data Link Physical addressing (MAC), frame formatting Ethernet, PPP, ARP MAC filtering, VLANs, ARP spoofing prevention 1 Physical Transmission of raw bits over media Cables, hubs, modems Physical security, tap detection

docs.title: IP Addressing
docs.text:
IP Address: An IP address (Internet Protocol address) is a unique numerical identifier assigned to each device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication.

It serves two critical purposes: identification (who the device is) and location addressing (where the device is in the network).

docs.title: Types of IP Addresses
docs.text:
1. IPv4 (32-bit) :

Address Length: 32 bits

Address Format: Dotted decimal (e.g., 192.168.0.1)

Total Addresses: ~4.3 billion (2³²)

Header Complexity: Simpler, fewer fields

Example Address: 192.0.2.1

Deployment: Widely used, but address exhaustion is an issue

Security: Relies on additional protocols (e.g., IPSec optional)

NAT (Network Address Translation): Commonly used to extend address space

2. IPv6 (128-bit)

Address Length: 128 bits

Address Format: Hexadecimal, colon-separated (e.g., 2001:0db8:85a3::8a2e:0370:7334)

Total Addresses: ~3.4×10³⁸ (2¹²⁸) — virtually unlimited

Header Complexity: More complex, but designed to be more efficient

Example Address: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329

Deployment: Increasing adoption; solves address exhaustion

Security: IPSec support is mandatory

NAT: Typically not needed; end-to-end connectivity is preferred

docs.title: Public & Private IP Range
docs.text:
Public IP Address : A public IP address is a globally unique IP address assigned to a device that needs to be accessible over the internet. Public IP addresses are assigned by Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) and regional Internet registries (RIRs) like ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC, and AFRINIC.

Usage: Typically used for servers, websites, and any other devices that need to be reachable from the internet.

Private IP Address: A private IP address used within a private network, such as a home or corporate network. These addresses are not routable on the global internet and are used for internal communication within a local network. Private IP addresses typically connect to the internet through a Network Address Translation (NAT) device, which maps the private IP addresses to a public IP address.

Usage: Used for devices within a private network to communicate with each other without using public IP addresses.

Range:

  • Class A: 10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255 (1 NETWORK)
  • Class B: 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 (16 NETWORKS)
  • Class C: 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255 (256 NETWORKS)

docs.title: Purpose:
docs.text:
• DHCP automates the process of assigning IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and other network configuration parameters to devices on a network.
  • It Provides administrators with a mechanism to dynamically allocate IP addresses, rather than manually setting the address on each device.

docs.title: Components:
docs.text: 1. DHCP Server: Manages a pool of IP addresses and configuration information. Assigns IP addresses and other settings to DHCP clients. 2. DHCP Client: A device requesting network configuration information from a DHCP server. 3. DHCP Relay Agent: Forwards DHCP messages between clients and servers when they are on different subnets.

docs.title: Process (DORA): Types of message—
docs.text:
There are four steps to this DHCP process :

1. Discover: Client broadcasts a DHCP Discover message to find available DHCP servers in local segment. 2. Offer: DHCP server responds with a DHCP Offer message, including an IP address and configuration parameters. 3. Request: Client sends a DHCP Request message to the selected DHCP server, requesting the offered IP address. 4. Acknowledge: DHCP server sends a DHCP Acknowledgment message, confirming the IP address assignment and providing configuration details.

docs.title: DHCP Lease time :
docs.text:
• IP Address Lease: DHCP servers assign IP addresses with a lease time. When the lease expires, the client must renew it.
  • Lease Renewal: Clients can request to renew their IP lease before it expires, ensuring continuity of service.
  • Lease Rebinding: If the original DHCP server is unreachable, the client may attempt to contact any available DHCP server for lease renewal.

docs.title: Configuration offered by DHCP Server :
docs.text:
In addition to IP address and subnet mask information, DHCP can provide the following protocol parameters:

  • Default Gateway
  • Domain Name
  • DNS servers
  • Time Servers
  • WINS servers

docs.title: Benefits:
docs.text:
• Centralized Management: Simplifies IP address management and configuration.
  • Reduced Manual Configuration: Minimizes the need for manual IP address assignments.
  • Dynamic Allocation: Efficiently manages IP address allocation and reuse.

docs.title: Security Considerations:
docs.text:
• Unauthorized DHCP Servers: Risk of rogue DHCP servers assigning incorrect settings. Use DHCP snooping to mitigate this risk.
  • IP Address Conflicts: Ensure proper configuration to avoid conflicts between statically and dynamically assigned addresses.

docs.title: Port Number:
docs.text:
• DHCP Client broadcast the DHCP discover message on port 67.
  • DHCP Server send the DHCP offer message port 68.

docs.title: Purpose:
docs.text:
• DHCP Relay allows DHCP clients on different subnets to communicate with a DHCP server that is not on the same local subnet.

  • This is essential in larger networks where a central DHCP server is used to manage IP address distribution across multiple subnets.

  • DHCP Relay Agent: A network device (usually a router or a switch) configured to forward DHCP requests and replies between clients and the DHCP server across different subnets.

  • Forwarding Mechanism: The relay agent listens for DHCP messages on its local interfaces and forwards them to the DHCP server's IP address.

docs.title: How DHCP Relay Works:
docs.text:
• DHCP Discover Message: A DHCP client broadcasts a DHCP Discover message on its local subnet.Relay
  • Agent Action: The relay agent intercepts this broadcast message and forwards it to the DHCP server, using unicast server.
  • Response: The DHCP server receives the message, processes it, and sends a DHCP Offer message back to the relay agent.
  • Relay Agent Forwarding: The relay agent receives the DHCP Offer and forwards it back to the client.
  • Client Request and Acknowledgment: The client then sends a DHCP Request message, and the server responds with a DHCP Acknowledgment, both of which are relayed by the DHCP relay agent.

docs.title: NAT Overload
docs.text:
NAT overload, also known as Port Address Translation (PAT) is a type of NAT that allows multiple devices on a local network to share a single public IP address when accessing the internet. This is achieved by translating private IP addresses and different port numbers to the public IP address.

When a device on the local network (with a private IP address) sends a request to the internet, the router or firewall translates the private IP and port number to the single public IP address. The router or firewall uses different port numbers for each device to distinguish between the connections.

Benefits:

Conserves public IP addresses: It allows multiple devices to use a single public IP address, reducing the need for multiple public IP addresses.

Improved security: Hides internal network addresses from the internet, enhancing security.

Limitations:

Potential performance issues: Can sometimes slow down performance, especially with multiple concurrent connections.

Can break end-to-end connectivity: Can make it difficult for external devices to directly connect to specific devices within the private network.

Compatibility issues with some applications: Some applications that rely on specific port numbers or require direct connections may not function correctly.

docs.title: NAT(Network Address Translation):
docs.text:
• Modify network address information in packet headers while they are in transit, which helps to map one IP address space into another.
  • NAT is commonly used to enable multiple devices on a local network to share a single public IP address.
  • Translate between private and public addresses
  • Translate multiple privately-addressed hosts to a single public address, which conserves the public address space.
  • Hiding the specific addresses and addressing structure of the internal (or private) network.
  • Public-to-public address translation, as well as private-to-private address translation.
  • Temporarily solution to the address shortage problem. IPv4 will eventually be replaced with IPv6

docs.title: Types of NAT :
docs.text:
Static NAT:

  • One-to-one translation between two addresses, or between a port on one address to a port on another address.
  • Maps one private IP address to one public IP address.
  • Often used to assign a public address to a device behind a NAT-enabled firewall/router.
  • Typically used for web servers or other devices that need to be accessible from outside the network.

Dynamic NAT:

  • Utilizes a pool of global addresses to dynamically translate the outbound traffic of clients behind a NAT-enabled device.

docs.title: NAT Overload or Port Address Translation (PAT) :
docs.text:
• Translates the outbound traffic of clients to unique port numbers off of a single global address.
  • PAT is necessary when the number of internal clients exceeds the available global addresses.

docs.title: NAT Terminology :
docs.text:
• Inside Local: The specific IP address assigned to an inside host behind a NAT-enabled device (usually a private address).
  • Inside Global: the address that identifies an inside host to the outside world (usually a public address). Essentially, this is the dynamically or statically-assigned public address assigned to a private host.
  • Outside Global: the address assigned to an outside host (usually a public address).
  • Outside Local: the address that identifies an outside host to the inside network. Often, this is the same address as the Outside Global. However, it is occasionally necessary to translate an outside (usually public) address to an inside (usually private) address.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text: Domain Name System (DNS) is a critical service that translates domain names (like www.google.com) into IP addresses (like 209.85.225.104). This translation is essential for connecting to resources on the Internet and within private networks.

docs.title: Purpose of DNS:
docs.text:
• DNS alleviates the need to remember numerical IP addresses by allowing users to use alphanumeric domain names.
  • It operates as a distributed hierarchical system, with servers responsible for different parts of the DNS namespace.

docs.title: Components of DNS:
docs.text:
• Hierarchy: DNS is structured hierarchically, from top-level domains (TLDs) like .com, to second-level domains (e.g., .google), and finally to hostnames (e.g., www).
  • DNS Servers:
    • Primary (Master) DNS Server: This server holds the original, authoritative copies of DNS records (zone files) for a domain. It manages updates to these records.
    • Secondary (Slave) DNS Server: This server maintains a copy of the primary server's zone files. It can answer queries if the primary server is unavailable and can also forward updates to the primary server.
    • Caching DNS Server: These servers do not store zone files but temporarily store (cache) resolved
    • DNS queries. They improve performance by reducing the need to query authoritative DNS servers repeatedly for the same information.

docs.title: Implementation and Configuration:
docs.text:
• HOSTS Files: These are local static files that can be configured on each device. They contain specific mappings of hostnames to IP addresses. Updates require manual changes on each device.
  • Centralized DNS Servers: Preferred in larger networks, all devices point to one or more DNS servers. Changes need to be made only on these servers, simplifying administration.

docs.title: Advantages of DNS over HOSTS Files
docs.text:
• Centralized Management: Changes are made once on DNS servers rather than on every device.
  • Scalability: Handles large volumes of DNS queries efficiently.
  • Redundancy and Load Balancing: DNS can distribute queries across multiple servers for fault tolerance and load balancing.

docs.title: Cabling & Connectors
docs.text:
Cabling and Connectors are the physical media and interfaces used to connect devices within a network, enabling data transmission.

  1. Ethernet Standards

Ethernet standards define the wiring and signaling for physical connections in a network. These standards include different speeds, transmission methods, and media types.

a. 10BASE-T

  • Speed: 10 Mbps (Megabits per second)
  • Cabling: Twisted-pair copper cable (Cat3 or higher)
  • Distance: Maximum of 100 meters per segment
  • Connector: RJ45
  • Usage: Early Ethernet networks, typically found in older infrastructure.

b. 100BASE-TX

  • Speed: 100 Mbps
  • Cabling: Twisted-pair copper cable (Cat5 or higher)
  • Distance: Maximum of 100 meters per segment
  • Connector: RJ45
  • Usage: Common in small and medium-sized networks during the late 1990s and 2000s, still in use in some legacy systems.

c. 1000BASE-T

  • Speed: 1 Gbps (Gigabit per second)
  • Cabling: Twisted-pair copper cable (Cat5e or Cat6)
  • Distance: Maximum of 100 meters per segment
  • Connector: RJ45
  • Usage: Widely used in modern networks, including offices and data centers.

d. 10GBASE-T

  • Speed: 10 Gbps
  • Cabling: Twisted-pair copper cable (Cat6a or Cat7)
  • Distance: Maximum of 100 meters per segment (Cat6a) or shorter distances for lower category cables
  • Connector: RJ45
  • Usage: High-speed network backbones, data centers, and environments requiring fast data transfer rates.

2. Fiber Optics

Fiber optic cables use light to transmit data, offering higher speeds and longer distances than copper cables. They are used in environments where high bandwidth, long-distance transmission, and resistance to electromagnetic interference (EMI) are required.

a. Single-Mode Fiber (SMF)

  • Core Diameter: Small core (typically 8-10 microns)
  • Light Source: Laser
  • Distance: Long distances, up to 40 km or more without the need for repeaters
  • Usage: Long-haul networks, metropolitan area networks (MANs), and high-speed data transmission over long distances.

b. Multi-Mode Fiber (MMF)

  • Core Diameter: Larger core (typically 50-62.5 microns)
  • Light Source: LED or laser
  • Distance: Shorter distances, up to 550 meters for 10 Gbps
  • Usage: Shorter-distance applications like LANs, data centers, and within buildings.

3. Connectors

Various connectors are used with copper and fiber optic cables to interface with network devices.

a. RJ45

  • Usage: The most common connector for twisted-pair Ethernet cables (Cat5, Cat6, etc.).
  • Features: 8 pins, supports various Ethernet standards from 10BASE-T to 10GBASE-T.

b. LC (Lucent Connector)

  • Usage: Commonly used with fiber optic cables, particularly in high-density patch panels.
  • Features: Smaller form factor, easy to use, with a push-pull latching mechanism.

c. SC (Subscriber Connector or Standard Connector)

  • Usage: Used in fiber optic networks, known for its square shape.
  • Features: Push-pull design, widely used in network environments, especially for single-mode fiber.

d. ST (Straight Tip)

  • Usage: Older fiber optic connector, commonly found in legacy systems.
  • Features: Bayonet-style connector, often used in multi-mode networks.

e. MTP/MPO (Multi-fiber Push On)

  • Usage: Used in environments requiring high fiber count, like data centers.
  • Features: Connects multiple fibers (12, 24, or more) in a single connector, allowing for higher-density connections.

docs.title: VLAN
docs.text:
Virtual LAN (VLAN) is a concept in which we can divide the devices logically on layer 2 (data link layer). Generally, layer 3 devices divide the broadcast domain but the broadcast domain can be divided by switches using the concept of VLAN.

Broadcast Domain:

A broadcast domain is a network segment in which if a device broadcast a packet then all the devices in the same broadcast domain will receive it. The devices in the same broadcast domain will receive all the broadcast packets but it is limited to switches only as routers don’t forward out the broadcast packet.

docs.title: VLANs offer several features and benefits, including:
docs.text:
• Improved network security: VLANs can be used to separate network traffic and limit access to specific network resources. This improves security by preventing unauthorized access to sensitive data and network resources.
  • Better network performance: By segregating network traffic into smaller logical networks, VLANs can reduce the amount of broadcast traffic and improve network performance.
  • Simplified network management: VLANs allow network administrators to group devices together logically, rather than physically, which can simplify network management tasks such as configuration, troubleshooting, and maintenance.
  • Flexibility: VLANs can be configured dynamically, allowing network administrators to quickly and easily adjust network configurations as needed.
  • Cost savings: VLANs can help reduce hardware costs by allowing multiple virtual networks to share a single physical network infrastructure.
  • Scalability: VLANs can be used to segment a network into smaller, more manageable groups as the network grows in size and complexity.

• VLAN tagging: VLAN tagging is a way to identify and distinguish VLAN traffic from other network traffic. This is typically done by adding a VLAN tag to the Ethernet frame header.

VLAN trunking: VLAN trunking allows multiple VLANs to be carried over a single physical link. This is typically done using a protocol such as IEEE 802.1Q

Access Port : Connecting to end devices (host or Router). Part of VLAN

Trunk Port : Do not belong to any VLAN. Carry Multiple VLAN Traffic. Link Between Two Switches. Also called Frame tagging.

  • VLANs is a switch-only feature. It works only on manageable Ethernet switches.
  • VLANs are used to create boundaries for broadcast messages.
  • VLANs do not share broadcast messages.
  • Devices in different VLANs cannot communicate directly. They can communicate through a router.
  • You can create and use the same VLAN on multiple routers. This feature allows you to arrange devices logically.
  • All switches have a default VLAN, called VLAN1.
  • By default, all switch ports belong to VLAN1.

docs.title: Ethernet Technology
docs.text:
What is Ethernet?

Ethernet is a family of technologies that provides data-link and physical specifications for controlling access to a shared network medium. It has emerged as the dominant technology used in LAN networking.

Ethernet was originally developed by Xerox in the 1970s, and operated at 2.94Mbps. The technology was standardized as Ethernet Version 1 by a consortium of three companies - DEC, Intel, and Xerox, collectively referred to as DIX - and further refined as Ethernet II in 1982.

In the mid-1980s, the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE) published a formal standard for Ethernet, defined as the IEEE 802.3 standard. The original 802.3 Ethernet operated at 10Mbps, and successfully supplanted competing LAN technologies, such as Token Ring.

Ethernet has several benefits over other LAN technologies:

  • Simple to install and manage
  • Inexpensive
  • Flexible and scalable
  • Easy to interoperate between vendors

Ethernet Cabling Types

Ethernet can be deployed over three types of cabling:

  • Coaxial cabling – almost entirely deprecated in Ethernet networking
  • Twisted-pair cabling
  • Fiber optic cabling

Coaxial Cable

Coaxial cable, often abbreviated as coax, consists of a single copper wire surrounded by insulation, a metallic shield, and a plastic sheath. The shield helps protect against electromagnetic interference (EMI), which can cause attenuation, a reduction of the strength and quality of a signal. EMI can be generated by a variety of sources, such as florescent light ballasts, microwaves, cell phones, and radio transmitters.

Coax is commonly used to deploy cable television to homes and businesses.

Twisted Pair Cable

Twisted-pair cable consists of two or four pairs of copper wires in a plastic sheath. Wires in a pair twist around each other to reduce crosstalk, a form of EMI that occurs when the signal from one wire bleeds or interferes with a signal on another wire. Twisted-pair is the most common Ethernet cable.

Twisted-pair cabling can be either shielded or unshielded. Shielded twisted pair is more resistant to external EMI; however, all forms of twisted-pair suffer from greater signal attenuation than coax cable.

There are several categories of twisted-pair cable, identified by the number of twists per inch of the copper pairs:

  • Category 3 or Cat3 - three twists per inch.
  • Cat5 - five twists per inch.
  • Cat5e - five twists per inch; pairs are also twisted around each other.
  • Cat6 – six twists per inch, with improved insulation.

Fiber Optics Cable

While coax and twisted-pair cabling carry electronic signals, fiber optics uses light to transmit a signal.

Ethernet supports two fiber specifications:

1. Single mode fiber – consists of a very small glass core, allowing only a single ray or mode of light to travel across it. This greatly reduces the attenuation and dispersion of the light signal, supporting high bandwidth over very long distances, often measured in kilometers. 2. Multimode fiber – consists of a larger core, allowing multiple modes of light to traverse it. Multimode suffers from greater dispersion than single mode, resulting in shorter supported distances.

  • Single mode fiber – consists of a very small glass core, allowing only a single ray or mode of light to travel across it. This greatly reduces the attenuation and dispersion of the light signal, supporting high bandwidth over very long distances, often measured in kilometers.
  • Multimode fiber – consists of a larger core, allowing multiple modes of light to traverse it. Multimode suffers from greater dispersion than single mode, resulting in shorter supported distances.

Single mode fiber requires more precise electronics than multimode, and thus is significantly more expensive. Multimode fiber is often used for high-speed connectivity within a datacenter.

The Ethernet Frame

An Ethernet frame contains the following fields:

Field Length Description Preamble 7 bytes Synchronizes communication Start of Frame 1 byte Signals the start of a valid frame MAC Destination 6 bytes Destination MAC address MAC Source 6 bytes Source MAC address 802.1Q tag 4 bytes Optional VLAN tag Ethertype or length 2 bytes Payload type or frame size Payload 42-1500 bytes Data payload CRC 4 bytes Frame error check Interframe Gap 12 bytes Required idle period between frames
  • Preamble (7 bytes): The preamble consists of a sequence of alternating 1s and 0s used to synchronize communication between the sending and receiving devices.
  • Start of Frame Delimiter (1 byte): This byte signals the start of a valid Ethernet frame, marking the boundary between the preamble and the frame data.
  • MAC Destination (6 bytes): The destination MAC address is the hardware address of the receiving device.
  • MAC Source (6 bytes): The source MAC address is the hardware address of the sending device.
  • 802.1Q tag (4 bytes): This optional field is used when VLAN tagging is required. It includes information about the VLAN ID and priority.
  • Ethertype or Length (2 bytes): This field either indicates the type of protocol encapsulated in the payload (e.g., IPv4, IPv6) or the length of the payload, depending on the frame type.
  • Payload (42-1500 bytes): The actual data being transported in the frame. The size can vary, but it typically ranges from 42 to 1500 bytes.
  • CRC (4 bytes): The Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) is used for error detection. It allows the receiving device to verify the integrity of the frame.
  • Interframe Gap (12 bytes): This is a required idle period between frames, allowing devices time to process the frame before the next one is sent.

CSMA/CD and Half-Duplex Communication

There are two methods of communication on a shared physical medium:

Half-Duplex – hosts can transmit or receive, but not simultaneously

Full-Duplex – hosts can both transmit and receive simultaneously

Ethernet in half-duplex mode uses the Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) protocol to manage communication between devices on a shared network medium. Here's how it works:

  • Carrier Sense: Before transmitting data, a device checks the network to ensure the medium is idle. If another device is already transmitting, the device waits until the medium is free.
  • Multiple Access: Multiple devices share the same network medium. Each device has the opportunity to transmit data, but only one device can do so at a time.
  • Collision Detection: If two devices transmit data simultaneously, a collision occurs, resulting in unreadable data. Both devices detect the collision and stop transmitting.
  • Collision Handling: After a collision, both devices send a 32-bit jam sequence to notify all devices on the network. They then wait for a random backoff time before attempting to retransmit, reducing the chance of another collision.
  • Slot Time: The slot time is the maximum duration within which a collision must be detected. For 10 and 100 Mbps Ethernet, the slot time is 512 bits (64 bytes), equivalent to the minimum frame size. For Gigabit Ethernet, the slot time is extended to 4096 bits.
  • Late Collisions: If a collision is detected after the slot time, it is called a late collision, typically indicating an issue with network length or configuration.

Full-Duplex Communication

Unlike half-duplex, full-duplex Ethernet supports simultaneously communication by providing separate transmit and receive paths. This effectively doubles the throughput of a network interface.

Full-duplex Ethernet was formalized in IEEE 802.3x, and does not use CSMA/CD or slot times. Collisions should never occur on a functional full duplex link. Greater distances are supported when using full-duplex over half-duplex.

Full-duplex is only supported on a point-to-point connection between two devices. Thus, a bus topology using coax cable does not support full-duplex. Only a connection between two hosts or between a host and a switch supports full-duplex. A host connected to a hub is limited to half-duplex. Both hubs and half-duplex communication are mostly deprecated in modern networks.

Categories of Ethernet

Ethernet standards, identified by numbers and letters (e.g., 802.3u, 802.3z), have evolved to support faster speeds, longer distances, and newer hardware.

Speed Categories

Ethernet: 10 Mbps

Fast Ethernet: 100 Mbps

Gigabit Ethernet: 1 Gbps

10 Gigabit Ethernet: 10 Gbps

Physical Standards

Labeling: E.g., 100baseT:

100: Transmission rate in Mbps

Base: Baseband transmission (single channel)

T - Media type (Twisted-pair)

Transmission:

Baseband: Single signal/channel per medium

Broadband: Multiple signals/channels via modulation

Ethernet(10 Mbps)

  • Originally referred to the 802.3 standard (10 Mbps).
  • Supports coax, twisted-pair, and fiber cabling.
  • Twisted-pair Ethernet uses two of the four pairs.

Common Ethernet Physical Standards:

IEEE Standard Physical Standard Cable Type Max Speed Max Length 802.3a 10base2 Coaxial (thinnet) 10 Mbps 185 meters 802.3 10base5 Coaxial (thicknet) 10 Mbps 500 meters 802.3i 10baseT Twisted-pair 10 Mbps 100 meters 802.3j 10baseF Fiber 10 Mbps 2000 meters

Full-Duplex:

  • 10baseT and 10baseF support full-duplex, doubling bandwidth to 20 Mbps.
  • Full-duplex is supported in point-to-point connections (e.g., between two hosts or a host and a switch).

Extending Ethernet Distance:

  • Repeater, hub, or switch can extend the maximum segment distance.

Fast Ethernet (100 Mbps)

  • EEE 802.3u (1995): Introduced Fast Ethernet at 100 Mbps.
  • Supports twisted-pair copper and fiber cabling.
  • Operates in half-duplex and full-duplex modes.

Common Fast Ethernet Physical Standards:

IEEE Standard Physical Standard Cable Type Max Speed Max Length 802.3u 100baseTX Twisted-pair 100 Mbps 100 meters 802.3u 100baseT4 Twisted-pair 100 Mbps 100 meters 802.3u 100baseFX Multimode fiber 100 Mbps 400-2000 meters 802.3u 100baseSX Multimode fiber 100 Mbps 500 meters
  • 100baseT4: Not widely implemented; supports only half-duplex.
  • 100baseTX: Dominant standard; uses two pairs in twisted-pair cables and requires Category 5 cable for reliability.

Speed and Duplex Auto negotiation

Compatibility:

Fast Ethernet (100 Mbps) is backward-compatible with the original Ethernet (10 Mbps). Devices supporting both are known as 10/100 devices.

Autonegotiation:

Fast Ethernet introduced autonegotiation to automatically select the best speed and duplex mode (full or half). Both sides of a connection must either autonegotiate or be hardcoded with identical settings to avoid duplex mismatches, which can cause severe performance issues.

Configuration Issues:

A duplex mismatch occurs if one side autonegotiates and the other is hardcoded, often leading to slow network performance due to collisions. Historically, early autonegotiation had standardization problems, leading to mistrust.

Current Best Practices:

Modern devices handle autonegotiation more reliably, but many administrators still prefer hardcoding settings, especially for servers. Gigabit Ethernet improved autonegotiation and generally recommends it as a best practice.

Gigabit Ethernet

Gigabit Ethernet operates at 1000 Mbps, and supports both twisted-pair (802.3ab) and fiber cabling (802.3z). Gigabit over twisted-pair uses all four pairs, and requires Category 5e cable for reliable performance.

Gigabit Ethernet is backwards-compatible with the original Ethernet and Fast Ethernet. A device that supports all three is often referred to as a 10/100/1000 device. Gigabit Ethernet supports both half-duplex or full duplex operation. Full-duplex Gigabit Ethernet effectively provides 2000 Mbps of throughput.

IEEE Standard Physical Standard Cable Type Speed Maximum Cable Length 802.3ab 1000baseT Twisted-pair 1 Gbps 100 meters 802.3z 1000baseSX Multimode fiber 1 Gbps 500 meters 802.3z 1000baseLX Multimode fiber 1 Gbps 500 meters 802.3z 1000baseLX Singlemode fiber 1 Gbps Several kilometers

10 Gigabit Ethernet

10 Gigabit Ethernet operates at 10000 Mbps, and supports both twisted-pair (802.3an) and fiber cabling (802.3ae). 10 Gigabit over twisted-pair uses all four pairs, and requires Category 6 cable for reliable performance.

IEEE Standard Physical Standard Cable Type Speed Maximum Cable Length 802.3an 10Gbase-T Twisted-pair 10 Gbps 100 meters 802.3ae 10Gbase-SR Multimode fiber 10 Gbps 300 meters 802.3ae 10Gbase-LR Single mode fiber 10 Gbps Several kilometers

10 Gigabit Ethernet is usually used for high-speed connectivity within a datacenter, and is predominantly deployed over fiber.

Twisted-Pair Cabling Overview

A typical twisted-pair cable consists of four pairs of copper wires, for a total of eight wires. Each side of the cable is terminated using an RJ45 connector, which has eight pins. When the connector is crimped onto the cable, these pins make contact with each wire.

docs.title: Wireless Concept
docs.text:
Wireless Concepts are essential for understanding how wireless networks operate, including the transmission of data, network identification, security, and the standards that govern wireless communication.

1. RF (Radio Frequency)

  • Function: Radio Frequency refers to the electromagnetic waves used to transmit data over wireless networks. RF is the core technology behind wireless communication, allowing devices to send and receive signals without physical connections.
  • Frequency Bands:
    • 2.4 GHz Band: Offers wider coverage but is more prone to interference from other devices like microwaves and Bluetooth. Supports 802.11b/g/n standards.
    • 5 GHz Band: Provides faster speeds and less interference but with a shorter range. Supports 802.11a/n/ac/ax standards.
  • Channel: RF spectrum is divided into channels. Proper channel selection can minimize interference and optimize performance.
  • Signal Strength and Quality:
    • RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator): Measures the power level of a received signal.
    • SNR (Signal-to-Noise Ratio): The difference between the signal strength and background noise; higher SNR means better quality.

2. SSID (Service Set Identifier)

  • Function: SSID is the name assigned to a wireless network. It helps users identify and connect to a specific network, especially in environments with multiple networks available.
  • Broadcasting:
    • Enabled (Default): The SSID is broadcasted, allowing devices to easily find and connect to the network.
    • Disabled: The SSID is hidden, requiring users to manually enter the network name to connect, which adds a layer of security.
  • Use Cases: In home and business networks, the SSID distinguishes one wireless network from another, making it easier for users to connect to the correct network.

3. Encryption

Encryption is critical for securing wireless networks by protecting the data transmitted between devices from being intercepted or tampered with. There are several encryption standards:

a. WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy)

  • Security Level: Low
  • Encryption: 40-bit or 104-bit key
  • Vulnerabilities: WEP is considered insecure due to flaws that make it easily crackable.
  • Use Cases: Legacy systems; not recommended for modern networks.

b. WPA (Wi-Fi Protected Access)

  • Security Level: Medium
  • Encryption: TKIP (Temporal Key Integrity Protocol)
  • Improvements Over WEP: Dynamic key generation and integrity checking, but still vulnerable to certain attacks.
  • Use Cases: Transitional standard; better than WEP but largely replaced by WPA2.

c. WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2)

  • Security Level: High
  • Encryption: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), which is more secure than TKIP.
  • Security Modes:
    • Personal Mode (WPA2-PSK): Uses a pre-shared key, suitable for home and small business networks.
    • Enterprise Mode (WPA2-EAP): Uses an authentication server (RADIUS), suitable for larger organizations requiring stronger security.
  • Use Cases: The most common and recommended standard for securing modern wireless networks.

d. WPA3

  • Security Level: Very High
  • Encryption: Improved encryption methods over WPA2, including better protection against brute-force attacks and enhanced security for public networks.
  • Use Cases: Emerging standard for future-proofing wireless networks with stronger security.

4. Wireless Standards (802.11)

Wireless standards are defined by the IEEE 802.11 family, specifying the protocols for wireless local area networks (WLANs).

a. 802.11a(1999)

  • Speed: Up to 54 Mbps
  • Frequency: 5 GHz
  • Range: Shorter range, less interference
  • Use Cases: Early adoption in corporate environments, now largely obsolete.

b. 802.11b

  • Speed: Up to 11 Mbps
  • Frequency: 2.4 GHz
  • Range: Wider range but susceptible to interference
  • Use Cases: Early home and small business networks; now outdated.

c. 802.11g

  • Speed: Up to 54 Mbps
  • Frequency: 2.4 GHz
  • Backward Compatibility: Compatible with 802.11b
  • Use Cases: Common in home and small business networks during the early 2000s.

d. 802.11n

  • Speed: Up to 600 Mbps (depending on configuration)
  • Frequency: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz (dual-band)
  • Technology: MIMO (Multiple Input, Multiple Output) for better performance and range
  • Use Cases: Widely used in both home and enterprise networks, offering better performance and range.

e. 802.11ac

  • Speed: Up to 1.3 Gbps or higher
  • Frequency: 5 GHz
  • Technology: Advanced MIMO, wider channels (up to 160 MHz), and beamforming for improved speed and reliability
  • Use Cases: Modern networks requiring high-speed wireless connections, such as streaming HD content and gaming.

f. 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6)

  • Speed: Up to 9.6 Gbps
  • Frequency: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz (dual-band, with potential for 6 GHz in Wi-Fi 6E)
  • Technology: OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access), MU-MIMO, better efficiency in crowded environments
  • Use Cases: Next-generation networks, ideal for environments with many connected devices (IoT, smart homes, offices).

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Routing is the process of sending a packet of information from one network to another network.

To do this, routers use Routing Tables, which contain:

  • The destination network and subnet mask
  • The “next hop” router to reach the destination
  • Routing metrics and Administrative Distance (AD)

docs.title: Types of Protocols in Routing
docs.text:
• Routed Protocols: These are Layer 3 protocols that assign logical addresses to devices and move data between networks.
    • Examples: IP, IPX
  • Routing Protocols: These build the network topology and determine the best path to each destination.
    • Examples: RIP, IGRP, OSPF

docs.title: Determining the Best Route
docs.text:
Routers decide the best route using three criteria, in this exact order:

  1. Prefix-Length

  2. The number of bits that identify the network.

  3. A longer prefix-length = more specific route.

  4. Example:

    Trying to reach 10.1.5.2/24

    • Routes in the table:
      • 10.1.5.0/24
      • 10.0.0.0/8
    • The router chooses 10.1.5.0/24 because it’s the most specific match.

  5. Metric

  6. Used within a routing protocol to choose the best path.

  7. Distance Vector protocols (e.g., RIP): Use hop count.
  8. Link State protocols (e.g., OSPF): Use a cost metric.
  9. Only the best metric route is inserted into the routing table.

  10. If multiple equal-metric paths exist, routers typically load-balance.

  11. Administrative Distance (AD)

  12. Used between routing protocols to decide which one to trust.

  13. Lower AD = More trusted
  14. If prefix-lengths are equal, AD determines the preferred route.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Routing is the process of sending a packet of information from one network to another network.

To route, routers build Routing Tables that contain the following:

  • The destination network and subnet mask
  • The “next hop” router to get to the destination network
  • Routing metrics and Administrative Distance

The routing table is concerned with two types of protocols:

  • A routed protocol is a layer 3 protocol that applies logical addresses to devices and routes data between networks. Examples would be IP and IPX.
  • A routing protocol dynamically builds the network, topology, and next hop information in routing tables. Examples would be RIP, IGRP, OSPF, etc.

Determining the best route by router :

To determine the best route to a destination, a router considers three elements (in this order):

  • Prefix-Length
  • Metric (within a routing protocol)
  • Administrative Distance (between separate routing protocols)

Prefix-length is the number of bits used to identify the network, and is used to determine the most specific route. A longer prefix-length indicates a more specific route. For example, assume we are trying to reach a host address of 10.1.5.2/24. If we had routes to the following networks in the routing table:

10.1.5.0/24

10.0.0.0/8

The router will do a bit-by-bit comparison to find the most specific route (i.e., longest matching prefix). Since the 10.1.5.0/24 network is more specific, that route will be used, regardless of metric or Administrative Distance.

Administrative Distance vs. Metric

A “metric” allows a router to choose the best path within a routing protocol. Distance vector routing protocols use “distance” (usually hop-count) as their metric. Link state protocols utilize some sort of “cost” as their metric.

Only routes with the best metric are added to the routing table. Thus, even if a particular routing protocol (for example, RIP) has four routes to the same network, only the route with the best metric (hop-count in this example) would make it to the routing table. If multiple equal-metric routes exist to a particular network, most routing protocols will load-balance.

If your router is running multiple routing protocols, Administrative Distance is used to determine which routing protocol to trust the most. Lowest administrative distance wins.

Again: if a router receives two RIP routes to the same network, it will use the routes’ metric to determine which path to use. If the metric is identical for both routes, the router will load balance between both paths.

If a router receives a RIP and an OSPF route to the same network, it will use Administrative Distance to determine which routing path to choose.

The Administrative Distance of common routing protocols (remember, lowest wins):

A route with an “unknown” Administrative Distance will never be inserted into the routing table.

The following command will allow you to view the routing table:

Router# show ip route

Routes are labeled based on what protocol placed them in the table:

C – Directly connected

S – Static

S* - Default route

D - EIGRP

R – RIP

I – IGRP

i – IS-IS

O - OSPF

Notice the RIP routes contain the following field: [120/1]. This indicates both the administrative distance and the metric (the 120 is the AD, and the 1 is the hop-count metric).

To clear all routes from the routing table, and thus forcing any routing protocol to repopulate the table:

Router# clear ip route *

Example:- Choosing the Best Route

Assume the following routes existed to the following host: 192.168.111.5/24

We have two RIP routes, an OSPF route, and a Static route to that destination. Which route will be chosen by the router?

Remember the three criteria the router considers:

  • Prefix-Length
  • Metric
  • Administrative Distance

The static route has the lowest administrative distance (1) of any of the routes; however, its prefix-length is less specific. 192.168.111.0/24 is a more specific route than 192.168.0.0/16. Remember, prefix-length is always considered first.

The second RIP route will not be inserted into the routing table, because it has a higher metric (5) than the first RIP route (1). Thus, our routing table will actually look as follows:

Thus, the true choice is between the OSPF route and the first RIP route. OSPF has the lowest administrative distance, and thus that route will be preferred.

PLEASE NOTE: Calculating the lowest metric route within a routing protocol occurs before administrative distance chooses the route it “trusts” the most. This is why the order of the above “criteria” is prefix-length, metric, and then administrative distance.

However, the route with the lowest administrative distance is always preferred, regardless of metric (assuming the prefix-length is equal). Thus, the metric is calculated first, but not preferred first over AD.

docs.title: 🧹 NETWORK SWEEPING
docs.text:
• Detecting live hosts using:
    • Ping sweeps: nmap -sn
    • ARP scans: nmap -PR (for local network)

docs.title: OS DISCOVERY
docs.text:
• Uses TCP/IP fingerprinting to detect target OS.
  • Run with nmap -O or -osscan-guess.

docs.title: NSE SCRIPTS
docs.text:
• Nmap Scripting Engine extends Nmap with custom scripts.
  • Categories:
    • auth, default, discovery, vuln, etc.
  • Example: nmap --script smb-os-discovery -p445 <target>

docs.title: SMB NULL SESSIONS
docs.text:
Allows unauthenticated users to access SMB info.

  • Use rpcclient -U "" <IP> or tools like enum4linux.

docs.title: ENUM4LINUX
docs.text:
Perl script for SMB/NetBIOS enumeration on Linux.

  • Gathers:
    • Users, Groups, Shares, OS info, password policies, etc.
  • Usage: enum4linux <IP>

docs.title: SMB NSE SCRIPTS
docs.text:
Nmap has specific scripts for SMB enumeration:

  • smb-enum-shares
  • smb-enum-users
  • smb-os-discovery
  • smb-vuln-ms17-010

docs.title: VRFY SCRIPT
docs.text:
SMTP VRFY command checks if a username is valid.

  • Syntax: VRFY user@example.com
  • Can be tested using telnet, nmap, or Python scripts.

docs.title: PYTHON PORT
docs.text:
• Python scripts can automate SMTP user enumeration.
  • Example:
import smtplib
server = smtplib.SMTP('mail.example.com', 25)
server.ehlo()
server.mail('test@example.com')
code, message = server.rcpt('admin@example.com')
if code == 250:
    print("User exists")

docs.title: SNMP MIB
docs.text:
• Management Information Base (MIB): database of objects SNMP can manage.
  • Helps interpret SNMP data (like sysName, sysDescr).

docs.title: SNMPWALK
docs.text:
• Command-line tool to query SNMP devices.
  • Example: snmpwalk -v2c -c public <IP>
  • Can retrieve:
    • System info, routing tables, interfaces, etc.

docs.title: NETCAT & NCAT
docs.text: Netcat and Ncat are both powerful networking utilities used for reading from and writing to network connections via TCP or UDP, but they have some key differences in features, syntax, and use cases.

docs.title: 🔹 Overview:
docs.text:
• Often referred to as the "Swiss Army knife of networking."
  • Very lightweight and widely available.
  • Comes in different versions (OpenBSD, GNU, traditional).

docs.title: 🔹 Features:
docs.text:
• Connect to or listen on TCP/UDP ports
  • File transfer
  • Simple chat server
  • Port scanning (basic)
  • Bind shell/reverse shell

docs.title: 🔹 Example Usage:
docs.text:
# Listen on port 1234
nc -l -p 1234

# Connect to a host
nc 192.168.1.10 1234

docs.title: 🔹 Overview:
docs.text:
• A modern reimplementation of Netcat, developed by the Nmap project.
  • More secure and feature-rich.
  • Cross-platform (Linux and Windows).

docs.title: 🔹 Enhanced Features:
docs.text:
• SSL/TLS support
  • Connection brokering (proxy via Ncat relay)
  • Input/output redirection
  • IPv6 support
  • Connection logging
  • Authentication

docs.title: 🔹 Example Usage:
docs.text:
# Listen with SSL
ncat --ssl -l 1234

# Connect using SSL
ncat --ssl target.com 1234

docs.title: 🔍 Key Differences:
docs.text: Feature Netcat (nc) Ncat SSL/TLS Support ❌ No ✅ Yes Cross-platform ❌ Limited ✅ Yes Maintained ⚠️ Some forks ✅ Actively (by Nmap) Input/output control ⚠️ Basic ✅ Advanced Authentication ❌ No ✅ Yes Relay/proxy mode ❌ No ✅ Yes

docs.title: Wireshark
docs.text: Wireshark is a free and open-source network protocol analyzer used for capturing and inspecting data traffic on a computer network in real time. It’s one of the most powerful tools for network troubleshooting, protocol analysis, penetration testing, and digital forensics.

docs.title: 🔍 Key Features of Wireshark:
docs.text:
• Live packet capture from network interfaces (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, etc.)
  • Deep inspection of hundreds of protocols (TCP, UDP, HTTP, DNS, etc.)
  • Color-coded filtering and highlighting for easy analysis
  • Packet reassembly for protocols like TCP
  • Exporting data for offline analysis (e.g., .pcap files)
  • Display filters for fine-grained inspection of traffic
  • Decryption support for many protocols (e.g., SSL/TLS if keys are available)

docs.title: 🛠️ Common Use Cases:
docs.text: Use Case Example Network troubleshooting Identify packet loss or latency issues Security analysis Detect suspicious packets or attacks Protocol development/testing Debug and verify custom protocols Malware analysis Inspect C2 traffic or exfiltration Educational purposes Learn how protocols like TCP/IP work

docs.title: 🔧 Basic Workflow:
docs.text:
1. Start Capture on a network interface.
  2. Apply Filters to narrow down the traffic (e.g., http, ip.addr == 192.168.1.1).
  3. Inspect Packets: View headers, payloads, and protocol details.
  4. Save or Export the capture for future analysis.

docs.title: 📦 Example Filters:
docs.text:
• ip.addr == 192.168.1.10 → Show traffic to/from that IP
  • tcp.port == 80 → Show HTTP traffic
  • http.request → Show HTTP requests only
  • dns → Show DNS queries/responses

docs.title: 📌 Note:
docs.text:
• Wireshark requires root/admin privileges to capture on some systems.
  • It can capture sensitive information (e.g., passwords in plain text protocols), so use it responsibly and legally.
